modules.title: Who is allowed to do what
modules.summary: The most common serious problem in web applications. It means a page or action that should be restricted can be reached by someone who should not reach it -- often just by editing the address bar.

items.title: Every private page and action requires signing in

risks.what: POST /api/admin/purge (server/src/api.ts line 12) has no sign-in check applied to it.
risks.impact: Anyone on the internet can call this address without an account. If it returns or changes anything that belongs to a particular person, they do not need to be that person to use it.
risks.fix: If this is meant to be public, mark it reviewed and move on. If not, apply your sign-in middleware to it -- ideally to the whole route prefix, so routes added later are protected automatically.

risks.what: GET /api/reports/:id (server/src/api.ts line 6) has no sign-in check applied to it.
risks.impact: Anyone on the internet can call this address without an account. If it returns or changes anything that belongs to a particular person, they do not need to be that person to use it.
risks.fix: If this is meant to be public, mark it reviewed and move on. If not, apply your sign-in middleware to it -- ideally to the whole route prefix, so routes added later are protected automatically.

risks.what: GET /api/preview (server/src/api.ts line 18) has no sign-in check applied to it.
risks.impact: Anyone on the internet can call this address without an account. If it returns or changes anything that belongs to a particular person, they do not need to be that person to use it.
risks.fix: If this is meant to be public, mark it reviewed and move on. If not, apply your sign-in middleware to it -- ideally to the whole route prefix, so routes added later are protected automatically.

items.title: Signed-in users can only see their own records
items.question: If one customer changed a number in the address bar, would they see another customer's data? Automated checks cannot tell whose record is whose -- only you know that.

items.title: File access cannot be steered outside its intended folder

modules.title: Protecting passwords, keys, and personal data
modules.summary: Covers secrets that should never be readable -- API keys, signing keys, passwords -- and sensitive data that should be protected in transit and at rest.

items.title: No keys or passwords are written into the code

risks.what: an LLM provider API key is written directly into your code (server/src/api.ts line 24).
risks.impact: This file contains what looks like an LLM provider API key. Anyone who can read the repository can use it as you. Because git keeps history, deleting the line later does not undo the exposure -- the key has to be revoked and reissued.
risks.fix: Revoke this credential with the provider first, then issue a new one and store it as an environment variable instead of committing it.

items.title: Passwords are stored using a slow, modern hash
items.question: Passwords must never be stored as typed, and never with a fast hash like MD5 or SHA-256. Confirm yours use argon2id or bcrypt -- deliberately slow algorithms that make guessing impractical.
items.notApplicable: This application does not appear to handle passwords.

items.title: You know what personal data this application stores
items.question: List what you collect that would matter if it leaked -- names, emails, payment details, health information. Some of it carries legal obligations.

modules.title: Visitor input being treated as instructions
modules.summary: Happens when something a visitor types is pasted into a command, a database query, or a page, and gets treated as an instruction rather than as text. This is the category the automated attack analysis targets most directly.

items.title: Database queries keep visitor input as data, not commands

risks.what: On GET /api/reports/:id, a value taken from the web address is used directly in a database query at server/src/api.ts line 8, with nothing in between checking that the value is what you expect.
risks.impact: Someone could read, change, or delete anything in your database -- including other people's accounts and personal information -- by typing carefully chosen text into your site.
risks.fix: Pass the value as a parameter instead of joining it into the query text -- the tagged `sql` template for postgres, or `?` placeholders with an argument array for mysql2. The database then treats it as data that can never be read as a command.
risks.evidence: req.param("id") → id → rows → `SELECT * FROM reports WHERE id = ${id}`

items.title: No system command is built from visitor input

risks.what: On POST /api/admin/purge, data sent by the visitor's browser is used directly in a command run on your server at server/src/api.ts line 14, with nothing in between checking that the value is what you expect.
risks.impact: Someone could run their own commands on the machine hosting your site, which usually means full control of it.
risks.fix: Pass the command and its arguments as a separate array rather than building one string, so the shell never interprets characters inside the value. Better still, use a library that does the job directly instead of running a command at all.

items.title: Visitor-supplied content cannot inject scripts into pages

risks.what: Raw HTML is inserted into the page without escaping (app/src/Profile.tsx line 4).
risks.impact: React normally neutralises HTML in your data so that text stays text. This line turns that protection off for one value. If that value ever contains something a user supplied, their markup -- including scripts that read logged-in sessions -- will run in your visitors' browsers.
risks.fix: If the content is plain text, render it as `{value}` and delete this prop. If it genuinely must be HTML, sanitise it with a library such as DOMPurify first.

modules.title: Gaps in how the feature was designed
modules.summary: Some problems are not mistakes in the code -- the code does exactly what it was asked to. These are gaps in what was asked for, so no automated tool can find them. They need your knowledge of how the product is supposed to work.

items.title: You have thought about how someone would deliberately misuse this
items.question: For each thing your app does, ask: what would someone gain by doing this a thousand times, out of order, or with values you did not expect?

items.title: Expensive or sensitive actions are rate limited
items.question: Anything that costs you money, sends a message, or checks a password should refuse to run thousands of times a minute from one source. Confirm which of your actions have a limit.

risks.what: None of the 3 routes in this application limits how often it can be called.
risks.impact: Without a limit, one person can call any address thousands of times a minute -- guessing passwords, running up costs on anything you pay per use, or simply making the site unavailable for everyone else.
risks.fix: Add a rate-limiting middleware to your routes, with a stricter limit on signing in and on anything that costs money to run.

items.title: Important rules are enforced on the server, not only in the browser
items.question: Anything checked only in the browser can be bypassed entirely -- the browser is the visitor's, not yours. Prices, limits, and permissions must be re-checked on the server.

modules.title: Settings that leave the door open
modules.summary: The code can be correct while the settings around it are not -- an overly permissive sharing rule, a debug mode left on, a default password never changed.

items.title: Only your own sites can call your API
Standard protective headers are switched on
items.question: Confirm your server sets the standard protective headers. They cost nothing and close a whole class of browser-side attacks.

risks.what: No protective response headers are configured in server/src/api.ts.
risks.impact: Browsers offer several protections that only switch on when your server asks for them -- refusing to let your site be framed by someone else's, and refusing to run scripts from places you did not approve. Without them, a small problem elsewhere in the site becomes a much larger one.
risks.fix: Add Hono's `secureHeaders()` middleware near the top of your server file. It is one line and needs no configuration to be useful.

items.title: The database is not reachable from the internet
items.question: Confirm your database does not publish a port to the outside world. It should be reachable only by your own application.
items.notApplicable: This project has no docker-compose file, so there is nothing to read.

items.title: Error messages shown to visitors do not reveal internals
items.question: A stack trace or raw database error tells an attacker how your system is built. Confirm visitors see a short message and the detail goes to your logs instead.

modules.title: Outdated or known-vulnerable building blocks
modules.summary: Your application is built on packages written by other people. When a security flaw is found in one of them, every application using it inherits the flaw until it is updated.

items.title: No dependency has a known published vulnerability
items.question: This needs a live vulnerability database, which is not wired up yet. Until it is, run your package manager's audit command and review what it reports.

items.title: No dependency is unmaintained or pulled from an unofficial source
items.question: A package that has not been updated in years will not be fixed when a flaw is found in it. Check the ones your app depends on most heavily.

items.title: Versions are pinned so builds are reproducible
items.question: Confirm your dependency versions are exact rather than ranges, so the code you reviewed is the code that ships.
items.notApplicable: No package.json was found in this project.

modules.title: Proving who someone is
modules.summary: Covers logging in, staying logged in, and logging out. Weaknesses here let someone become another user, which makes every other permission check meaningless.

items.title: Login tokens cannot be read by scripts on the page
Sessions expire and can be revoked
items.question: Confirm a login does not last forever, and that signing out actually invalidates it on the server rather than only in the browser.
items.notApplicable: No login tokens are issued by this application.

items.title: Repeated failed logins are slowed down or blocked
items.question: Without a limit, someone can try millions of passwords against one account. Confirm repeated failures are slowed, locked, or challenged.

items.title: Password reset cannot be used to take over an account
items.question: Reset links must expire, be single-use, and be sent only to the address already on the account. This is the most commonly abused way into an account.

modules.title: Trusting code and data that could have been tampered with
modules.summary: Covers where your code comes from and whether anything could alter it on the way -- an unpinned dependency, an unsigned update, data accepted from elsewhere without checking.

items.title: A lockfile records exactly which package versions are installed
items.question: Confirm a lockfile is committed. Without one, two installs of the same code can pull different package versions.
items.notApplicable: No package.json was found in this project.

items.title: Automated build steps cannot be modified by contributors
items.question: Your build pipeline usually holds deployment credentials. Confirm who is able to change what it runs.

items.title: Data from outside is validated before being used
items.question: Data arriving from another system is no more trustworthy than data typed by a visitor. Confirm it is checked against an expected shape before use.

modules.title: Noticing when something goes wrong
modules.summary: If an attack succeeds and nobody notices, it continues. The average intrusion goes undetected for months. This module is about being able to tell that something happened, and when.

items.title: Logins, failures, and permission denials are recorded
items.question: Confirm you record who signed in, what failed, and what was refused. Without it there is no way to reconstruct an incident afterwards.

items.title: Logs never contain passwords, tokens, or keys
items.question: Logs are copied, shipped to other services, and read by more people than your database. Confirm nothing sensitive is written into them.

items.title: Someone would actually see an alert
items.question: A log nobody reads is not monitoring. Decide who gets notified, and for what.

modules.title: Your server being tricked into fetching things
modules.summary: If your application fetches a web address that a visitor supplies, they can point it at systems only your server can reach -- internal dashboards, cloud configuration services -- and read the reply.

items.title: Visitor-supplied addresses are checked against an allowlist

risks.what: On GET /api/preview, a value from the part of the address after the question mark is used directly in a request your server makes to another address at server/src/api.ts line 20, with nothing in between checking that the value is what you expect.
risks.impact: Someone could make your server fetch addresses of their choosing, including private systems on your own network that the outside world cannot normally reach.
risks.fix: Check the address against a list of destinations you allow before fetching it, and refuse anything pointing at a private network address -- including the cloud metadata address, which hands out credentials.

items.title: Requests to private network addresses are blocked
items.question: Confirm your server refuses to fetch addresses on your own private network, including the cloud metadata address that hands out credentials.
